opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The frame I keep coming back to is that at some point, maybe not that far off, we'll have AI systems that can do most of the intellectual work that currently happens in AI safety, policy, and science more broadly, and do it faster and probably better than we can. So the question for us now is: what has to be in place *before* that point, because we can't just hand it off to the AIs later?

A few things stand out to me.

First, anything that's on the critical path to actually *trusting* those systems. If you're going to delegate alignment research to AIs, you need some way of knowing whether they're doing it in good faith. So work on evaluations, especially dangerous-capability and propensity evals, interpretability, control-style setups where you assume the model might be adversarial and still try to extract useful work safely, all of that seems really high priority, because it's the infrastructure that lets you use the AI help at all.

Second, things that are slow because of humans and institutions, not because of thinking. AIs can write a policy memo in seconds, but they can't make a government build the capacity to understand frontier AI, or get labs to agree to share information, or build public trust. Those processes take years of relationship-building and precedent-setting. So I'd push a lot of effort toward institutional capacity, transparency requirements, and getting early warning systems in place, so that when things start moving fast, there are people in positions to notice and respond.

Third, and this one's a bit subtler, I think we should be investing in figuring out what we'd even want to ask the AIs to do. If you get a sudden surge of very capable cognitive labor, the bottleneck shifts to having good questions, good priorities, and good ways of checking answers. Thinking through "if we had a million competent researchers for a month, what would we have them work on, and how would we verify it?" is actually a pretty useful exercise right now.

And conversely, I'd somewhat deprioritize work that looks like detailed object-level research that AIs will just blow past in a couple of years. Not that it's worthless, it builds skills and understanding, but if a problem is well-specified and easy to verify, that's exactly the kind of thing that's likely to get automated first. The comparative advantage of humans right now is in the messy, hard-to-verify, coordination-heavy stuff, and in setting things up so the transition goes well rather than chaotically.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes messy, hard-to-verify, coordination-heavy work, where it says humans have a comparative advantage over AI.

r002.rationale: It identifies institutional capacity, trust, and relationship-building as preparations that take years and should begin before AI capabilities accelerate.

r003.rationale: It says institutional processes can take years, but does not state that a policy idea takes years to become a readily available option in society’s thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that a lot of the most important work is work that doesn't feel very glamorous right now, because it's about setting ourselves up to be in a good position later rather than solving the hard problem directly today.

The way I think about it is: at some point we're going to have systems that are better than us at AI research, at understanding their own training process, at anticipating what we're going to check for. And at that point, a lot of the techniques we'd naively want to use, like just reading the outputs and seeing if they look good, stop being reliable on their own. So the question is, what can we do now, while the systems are still roughly at or below our level, that pays off then?

I'd put it in maybe three buckets.

The first is just measurement and evaluation. We should be building really good tests for the capabilities we're worried about, and for alignment-relevant properties, while the models are still weak enough that we can trust the tests. That includes dangerous capability evals, but also evals for things like "does this model behave differently when it thinks it's being watched," or "can it sandbag." Even if the current systems can't do those things, getting the infrastructure and the muscle memory in place means that when the capability does show up, we notice it rather than being surprised.

The second bucket is what I'd call scalable oversight, or more broadly, techniques for using AI to help us supervise AI. I think the realistic path is not that humans stay in full control through unaided judgment. It's that we find ways to use weaker, more trusted systems, or carefully constrained versions of stronger systems, to check the stronger systems' work. Things like debate, or decomposing tasks so each piece is checkable, or using models to help us find the places where another model's reasoning is suspicious. The key point is that these techniques need to be developed and stress-tested while we can still verify the results ourselves, because that's the only window where we can tell whether they actually work.

And the third bucket, which I think is underrated, is just the institutional and organizational side. Who gets to decide when a model is safe to deploy? What does the decision process look like inside a lab when the model is producing most of the research? What commitments have been made ahead of time about what you'd do if an eval comes back red? A lot of the failure modes I worry about aren't that no one had the technical tool. It's that there was enormous commercial pressure, the tool gave an ambiguous answer, and the decision got made by people who were already committed to shipping. So pre-committing to decision rules, building external auditing capacity, having people whose job is explicitly to be the skeptic, that all matters a lot.

If I had to pick one thing to emphasize, it would be that the window where we can check our safety techniques against ground truth is finite, and it's closing. So the prioritization should lean heavily toward stuff that builds verified trust now, rather than stuff that assumes we'll be able to figure it out once the systems are smarter. Because by then the systems might be the ones figuring it out, and we'd like to already know whether we can believe them.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes work that can be verified while systems are weaker, but does not say this work is something future advanced AIs will be comparatively disadvantaged at doing.

r002.rationale: It recommends building evaluation infrastructure and decision processes in advance, but does not identify inherently long setup times as the reason to prepare before advanced AIs arrive.

r003.rationale: It discusses precommitting to deployment rules, but does not say that policy ideas can take years to become readily available in society’s thinking.

astra-6.text:
I think we should focus on the things we need to get right before we can safely delegate more of the work to AI. There’s a tempting thought that, if the systems are going to understand all of this much better than we do, we should just wait and ask them what to do. But that leaves a pretty crucial question: how do we know we can trust their advice?

So I’d put a lot of emphasis on being able to evaluate these systems, understand what kinds of risks they pose, and have a process for deciding when it’s safe to give them more autonomy. That includes technical work on oversight, but also institutions that can actually act on the results—slow down a deployment, require additional testing, or limit what a system can do.

And I’d distinguish between work where a mistake is relatively easy to correct later and work that determines whether we retain the ability to correct mistakes at all. Future AI could help enormously with scientific research and even with alignment research. But the conditions under which we bring that help into the picture seem especially important to work on now. We want to get to a place where more capable AI expands our ability to make good decisions, and where we have evidence that relying on it is warranted.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes evaluating AI systems and building institutions, but does not say these are tasks future AIs will be comparatively disadvantaged at doing.

r002.rationale: It argues that preparation should happen now, but does not identify inherently long setup times as a reason that human preparation is valuable.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention years for a policy idea to become readily available in society’s thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should prioritize work that helps us stay in control of the process as AI systems become more capable. It’s tempting to say, “Well, the smarter systems will help us solve alignment,” and I do expect AI assistance to be really valuable. But there’s a bootstrapping problem: we need to be able to trust the systems that are helping us, and evaluate whether their proposed solutions actually work.

So one priority is figuring out how to get useful work out of a system without assuming that we can understand everything it’s doing. Can we check its outputs? Can we structure the task so that a mistake or an attempt to deceive us is likely to be caught? Can we use other AI systems to help with that oversight without just moving the same problem somewhere else?

And then I’d put a lot of weight on having the ability to slow down when we don’t have good answers. That means evaluations that inform real deployment decisions, and institutions that can actually act on those evaluations. If a system understands the situation much better than we do, we don’t want our entire safety plan to depend on noticing something worrying in a conversation with it.

The common thread is preserving our ability to make meaningful choices. We should use the capabilities we have now to make the next stage safer, rather than assuming that greater capability will automatically bring greater control.

r001.rationale: The response recommends work on oversight, evaluations, and maintaining control, but does not say to prioritize tasks future advanced AIs will be comparatively worse at doing.

r002.rationale: It says to use current capabilities to make the next stage safer, but does not identify long setup times as a reason to prepare before advanced AIs arrive.

r003.rationale: The response discusses evaluations and institutions, but does not state that policy ideas can take years to become readily available in society’s thinking.
